Recalcitrance means stubborn, persistent refusal to obey, cooperate, or follow what is expected — especially when someone in authority is asking you to do something. It is the quality of digging your heels in and refusing to budge, no matter what.

Think of a child who is told to go to bed, and instead of going, they cross their arms, sit on the floor, and simply refuse — not because they can't go to bed, but because they won't. That attitude, that defiant, unyielding resistance, is recalcitrance.
What makes it more than just stubbornness

Stubbornness is a broad word. You can be stubborn about your favourite food, or stubborn about a preference. Recalcitrance is more specific and stronger. It almost always involves resistance to authority, rules, control, or correction. There is a flavour of defiance in it — a sense that the person knows what is being asked of them and is actively, consciously choosing not to comply.

It also implies persistence. It is not a one-time refusal. Recalcitrance is a pattern or a quality — a sustained, ongoing resistance that is difficult to break through.

Recalcitrance has a negative tone. When someone describes a person's behaviour as recalcitrance, they are not impressed by it. They are frustrated by it. The word suggests that the resistance is unreasonable, obstinate, and difficult to deal with. It often makes the person showing it appear troublesome, uncooperative, or even rebellious.
Who or what can show recalcitrance

Most commonly, the word is used for people. A student who repeatedly ignores a teacher's instructions shows recalcitrance. An employee who refuses to follow company policies despite repeated warnings shows recalcitrance. A prisoner who consistently defies the rules of a correctional facility shows recalcitrance.

But the word can also apply to organisations, governments, or even groups. A government that repeatedly refuses to follow international agreements despite pressure from other nations can be said to show recalcitrance. A company that refuses to cooperate with a regulatory investigation shows recalcitrance.

Interestingly, animals can also be described this way, though less formally. A horse that refuses to move when its rider urges it forward shows recalcitrance. This is actually a classic image tied to the spirit of the word.

Compared to defiance, recalcitrance is more passive and internal. Defiance is loud and outward — shaking your fist at someone. Recalcitrance is more like a wall — silent, immovable, unresponsive.

Compared to reluctance, recalcitrance is far stronger. Reluctance means you don't really want to do something but you might do it anyway. Recalcitrance means you are not doing it, full stop.

Compared to disobedience, recalcitrance is deeper and more habitual. A child might disobey once. But recalcitrance suggests a settled, repeated pattern of not cooperating — it is almost a personality trait or a defining stance, not just a single act.

You will most often encounter this word in formal writing — journalism, legal documents, academic texts, or political commentary. Here are a few natural examples of how it appears:

"The government's recalcitrance in the face of public pressure was astonishing."

"Her recalcitrance frustrated every teacher who tried to help her."

"The committee expressed concern about the organisation's recalcitrance in meeting its obligations."

"Despite months of negotiation, his recalcitrance made any agreement impossible."
The single sentence to remember it by
If you ever want to recall this word quickly, think of it this way: Recalcitrance is what you call it when someone refuses to cooperate with authority, again and again, no matter what.
